prompt: What do you know about https://www.rover.com/?
answer:
is a  pet-care marketplace —essentially a platform that connects pet owners with independent pet sitters, dog walkers, and other pet-care providers.
Here’s the useful overview:
• Founded:  2011. Rover started primarily around dog sitting/walking and has expanded into a broader pet-care marketplace.
• Services:  boarding in a sitter's home, house sitting in your home, doggy day care, dog walking, drop-in visits, and—in the U.S.—in-person dog training.
• How it works:  You search by location and dates, compare sitter profiles/reviews/prices, message candidates, optionally arrange a Meet & Greet, and then book/pay through Rover.
• Trust & safety:  Rover says sitters undergo identity verification  or background checks depending on the market, bookings have protection/guarantees subject to the applicable terms, and Rover provides support.
• Scale:  Rover currently says its group operates in  18 countries , has cared for  12+ million pets , and has facilitated  41 million 5-star stays/bookings .
• It's no longer publicly traded:  Private-equity funds affiliated with  Blackstone  completed a roughly  $2.3 billion acquisition  of Rover in February 2024, after which Rover's Nasdaq  listing ended.
• Expansion:  Rover has been building a broader international pet-care group. It acquired  Cat in a Flat  in 2024, announced  the acquisition of  Mad Paws  in Australia in 2025, and acquired  Meowtel  in January 2026.
One important caveat
Rover isn't itself  a traditional kennel or pet-care company.  It's a marketplace.  The individual sitter is the person actually providing the care, so the quality can vary substantially from one provider to another. Rover itself recommends checking reviews,  communicating expectations, and doing a Meet & Greet before booking.
If you're asking because you're  considering using Rover, becoming a Rover sitter, or evaluating Rover as a business/company , I  can dig much deeper into whichever angle you're interested in—including  how Rover makes money, its fees/commission structure, business model, competitors, reputation, or whether it's available in Bali/Indonesia .

prompt: What do you know about Rover (https://www.rover.com/)?
answer:
is a  pet-care marketplace and technology platform  that connects pet owners with independent pet sitters, dog walkers, and other care providers.
What Rover does
Rover essentially acts as a marketplace between two sides:
• Pet parents  can find and book local caregivers.
• Sitters/walkers  can create profiles, set their rates and availability, and acquire customers through Rover.
• Services include  dog boarding, house sitting, doggy day care, dog walking, drop-in visits, dog training , and—in some markets—grooming.
• Customers can look at  profiles, reviews, availability and experience, communicate through Rover, arrange a Meet & Greet, and pay through the platform.
So conceptually, it's somewhat like  Airbnb/Uber for pet care , although the actual service is much more relationship-driven and often involves repeat bookings.
How the business works
The interesting part of Rover isn't really the pet sitting itself—it's the  marketplace infrastructure around it .
Rover provides:
• Discovery/search and matching
• Profiles and reviews
• Identity/background screening
• Messaging
• Scheduling and payments
• Customer acquisition for sitters
• Trust & safety mechanisms
• Booking protection/Rover Guarantee
• 24/7 support
• Mobile apps and photo updates
Rover says its marketplace has facilitated  12+ million pets cared for , operates in  18 countries , and has an average sitter rating of  4.9/5 . Features and protections vary by market.
Sitters are effectively small businesses operating through the marketplace: they choose services, rates, availability and pet preferences, then  go through Rover's onboarding process, including identity verification/background checks and a safety quiz.
Ownership
One important thing that has changed:  Rover is no longer a publicly traded company.
In February 2024, private-equity firm  Blackstone  completed its acquisition of Rover in an all-cash transaction valued at approximately  $2.3 billion . Rover's stock was subsequently delisted from Nasdaq .
Rover had previously been a public company under the ticker  ROVR .
Why Rover is interesting
From a business/strategy perspective, Rover is a  particularly interesting marketplace because  trust is the product as much as the software is .
Someone isn't simply buying a 30-minute walk. They're giving a stranger access to their  home and/or an animal they consider part of their family . That makes things such as reviews, repeat customers, background checks, identity verification, Meet & Greets, insurance/pro tection and reputation extremely important.
It also has a potentially attractive  repeat-purchase dynamic : once a pet owner finds a sitter they trust, they may use that same person repeatedly for walks, weekends away, holidays,  etc. Rover explicitly encourages this continuity across services.
If you're asking because you're  researching Rover as a company/business model — for example, its revenue model, take rate, unit economics, competitors, market size, valuation, or how you might build something similar—I can break that down in considerably more depth.

answer:
If you mean  Rover (@roverdotcom) , the  large pet-care brand, it’s much more than an Instagram account. It’s the consumer-facing brand of  Rover Group , a Seattle-based pet-care marketplace founded in 2011.
What Rover actually does
Rover connects  pet parents  with independent pet-care providers. Depending on the market, people can book:
• Dog boarding
• House sitting
• Doggy day care
• Dog walking
• Drop-in visits
• Dog training
• Grooming in some markets
For sitters, the proposition is essentially:  use Rover to find clients and run a small pet-care business.  Sitters set their own profiles and pricing and are independent contractors rather than Rover employees.
How big is it?
Rover says its marketplaces now operate across  18 countries , with  12+ million pets cared for ,  41 million 5-star stays , and an average sitter rating of  4.9/5 .
The company was taken private by  Blackstone in 2024 , after having been publicly traded on Nasdaq.
It has also been expanding beyond the original Rover marketplace. In January 2026, Rover announced its acquisition of  Meowtel , a cat-sitting marketplace, adding  a more cat-specific offering to its portfolio.
And the Instagram account?
@roverdotcom is the brand's official Instagram presence  and is essentially the social-media expression of the Rover brand: lots of dogs/cats, pet-parent culture, humorous/relatable pet content, and content designed to make Rover synonymous with the emotional side of having pets—not merely with booking a dog walker .
One interesting thing about Rover's marketing is that  the product is relatively utilitarian, while the brand is highly emotional . Rover isn't just selling "dog sitting";  its stated mission is about making it easier for people to experience the love of pets.
That distinction is important if you're  asking because you're  researching the account/brand itself —for example, its content strategy, audience, influencer strategy, partnerships, or whether there's a business opportunity around it. is a major pet-care marketplace, and  @roverdotcom  is its official consumer-facing Instagram brand account.

In the U.S., Rover currently says pet parents pay an  11% booking fee , while providers generally pay a  20% service fee , meaning providers take home 80% of their booking revenue. There are some location- and provider-specific variations/pilots.
That creates a classic marketplace flywheel:
more pet parents → more bookings → more attractive platform for sitters → more sitter supply → better selection → more pet parents.
Rover also gets considerable value from keeping communication and payment on-platform, because that's where it can provide its protections and monetize the transaction.
Trust & safety is a huge part of the proposition
Pet care has an unusual marketplace problem: you're not merely buying a service—you're entrusting someone with an animal, sometimes  inside your home .
Rover therefore puts considerable emphasis on:
• background checks / identity verification
• verified reviews
• in-platform messaging
• secure payments
• Meet & Greets
• 24/7 support
• the  Rover Guarantee / RoverProtect  framework
Rover says its Guarantee can provide reimbursement for eligible veterinary costs, with the U.S. consumer site currently advertising up to  $25,000  in eligible vet-care reimbursement.
That trust layer is strategically important: Rover isn't just selling convenience; it's trying to make an inherently high-trust transaction feel safe enough to do online.
Ownership changed significantly
One important corporate detail:  Rover is no longer a publicly traded company.
In February 2024, private-equity funds affiliated with  Blackstone  completed their acquisition of Rover in an all-cash transaction valued at approximately  $2.3 billion . Rover's public stock was subsequently delisted from Nasdaq.
Rover is now part of the broader  Rover Group , which says it also includes  Cat in a Flat  and  Mad Paws .
The Instagram/brand angle
If you're asking because you're interested in  Rover as a social-media brand , that's particularly interesting.
Their marketing territory is naturally rich: pets provide an almost endless supply of emotionally engaging content. But Rover's strongest differentiation isn't simply  “look at these cute dogs.”  It's the broader emotional proposition:
We understand your pet.
That's a much stronger brand position because it speaks to the anxiety and emotional attachment behind purchasing pet care.
Their current creative direction reflects this: Rover is increasingly portraying pets as individuals with preferences, quirks, personalities and inner lives—not just animals who need food, walks and supervision.
And the company's own press activity shows that  content and cultural relevance are part of its marketing strategy , not merely PR. Its 2026 press room includes research around dog breeds, pet-parent trends, sports viewing, travel and the cost of pet parenthood.
In one sentence
Rover is a two-sided pet-care marketplace that has evolved into a large consumer pet brand, using trust/safety infrastructure to facilitate transactions while building emotional affinity around the idea that every pet deserves care tailored to who they are.
If you're looking at Rover for  competitive research, brand strategy, social-media analysis, partnership/influencer opportunities, or as a potential customer/provider , I can also break down its  business model, target audience, Instagram strategy, competitors, brand voice, and what makes the brand successful .

prompt: What do you know about https://www.rover.com/ in Washington?
answer:
If by  Washington  you mean  Washington, D.C. ,
is a large online marketplace that connects pet owners with independent pet sitters and dog walkers.
What Rover offers in Washington, D.C.
• Dog walking  — typically 30-minute neighborhood walks. Rover currently shows an average of about  $22.20 per walk  in D.C., although individual walkers set their own prices.
• Dog boarding  — your dog stays overnight at the sitter's home. Current D.C. listings include sitters starting around  $40–$50/night , with substantial variation.
• House sitting  — the sitter stays at your home with your pet. Current listings I found start around  $55–$65/night  for some sitters.
• Drop-in/pet sitting  — a sitter visits your home to feed, play with, walk, or otherwise care for your pet. Rover currently reports an average of about  $23.54 per visit  for pet sitting in D.C.
• Doggy daycare  is also available.
Is Rover reputable?
Generally, yes. Rover is an established marketplace rather than a traditional pet-care company where all employees work directly for Rover. You select an individual sitter/walker through the platform.
Rover says its screened sitters undergo a  third-party background check , bookings are paid through the platform, and eligible bookings have protection through the  Rover Guarantee . It also provides 24/7 support.
One important point:  the individual sitter matters enormously.  I'd look closely at their number of completed bookings, reviews, repeat clients, experience with your type of pet, cancellation history, and whether they offer a meet-and-greet before booking.
If you're considering Rover as a sitter
That's a different proposition. Rover also recruits people in Washington, D.C. to provide dog walking, boarding, house sitting and drop-in services. You set your own schedule and rates, while Rover handles booking/payment infrastructure and provides support.
If you tell me what you mean by  “in Washington” —for example,  using Rover to find a dog sitter, becoming a Rover sitter, or evaluating Rover as a business/company —I can go much deeper into the relevant part.

prompt: What do you know about https://www.rover.com/ in United States?
answer:
Yes.
is a major U.S.  pet-care marketplace  that connects pet owners with independent pet sitters, dog walkers, and other pet-care providers.
What Rover is
Rover was founded in  2011  and operates as a marketplace rather than a traditional pet-care company. Pet owners search for providers in their area, communicate with them through Rover, and book/pay through the platform.
Services include:
• Dog boarding  — your dog stays at the sitter's home
• House sitting  — the  sitter stays at your home
• Doggy day care
• Dog walking
• Drop-in visits
• Dog training
• Grooming  in some markets
Rover says its marketplace has facilitated care for  12+ million pets  and has accumulated  41 million 5-star stays , although these are company-reported figures.
How it works for a pet owner
Typically, you:
Enter your location and pet-care dates.
Compare providers based on price, reviews , experience and availability.
Message the provider.
Arrange a  Meet & Greet .
Book and pay through Rover.
Receive updates/photos during the booking.
An important point is that  sitters generally set their own rates , so prices can vary substantially by city, service, experience, holidays and additional pets.
Is Rover safe?
Rover has several safety mechanisms, but I'd distinguish  "Rover screens providers" from "every provider is guaranteed to be excellent."
Rover says U.S./North American sitters and dog walkers undergo third-party background screening, and profiles can display background-check badges. It also provides  verified reviews, in-platform communication, 24/7 support and the Rover Guarantee for eligible situations.
However, Rover's own terms make clear that background checks have limitations and are performed by third parties; Rover doesn't guarantee that a background check is complete or perfectly accurate.
So if you're hiring someone, I'd still recommend checking their reviews, repeat-client history, experience with your particular type of pet, and  doing a Meet & Greet.
What does Rover cost?
For U.S. pet owners, Rover currently says its  booking fee is 11% , although California has different fee rules. The sitter's listed price is separate from the booking fee.
For providers, Rover generally says it takes a  20% service fee , leaving the sitter with 80% of the booking revenue, although Rover notes that some U.S. providers may be participating in a fee pilot with different terms.
For example, if a sitter 's service price is $100, the economics aren't simply "the sitter gets $100": Rover's provider fee and the owner's booking fee are separate components.
Rover as a business
Rover is particularly interesting because it essentially operates a  two-sided marketplace :
Pet owners → Rover → independent pet-care providers
Rover supplies the marketplace, search/discovery, reviews, payment processing, trust/safety infrastructure, customer support and certain protections, while the actual pet care is provided by the individual sitter/w alker.
The company is now part of  The Rover Group , which also includes Cat in a Flat and Mad Paws.
One thing worth noting if you're evaluating Rover commercially: its current Terms  of Service, effective  August 17, 2026 , contain a binding arbitration provision and class-action/jury-trial waiver, subject to the terms  and opt-out provisions described there.
If you're asking because you're considering using Rover
I  can also dig deeper into  Rover in the U.S. from a business/competitive perspective —for example, its revenue model, fees , sitter economics, customer acquisition, competitors like Wag!, market size, pros/cons, and whether Rover is a good platform for  starting a pet-sitting business .

prompt: What do you know about https://www.rover.com/?
answer:
is a large online marketplace for  pet care , primarily connecting pet  owners with independent sitters, walkers, and trainers.
What Rover does
Rover lets pet owners search for and book services such as:
• 🐕  Dog walking
• 🏠 House sitting  — the sitter stays at your home
• 🐶  Boarding  — the pet stays at the sitter's home
• ☀️  Doggy day care
• 🐾  Drop-in visits
• 🎓  Dog training
• 🛁 In some  markets,  grooming/bathing services
The exact services available depend on the country and local market.
How the marketplace works
It's essentially a  two-sided marketplace :
Pet owner → Rover → independent pet-care provider
Owners create a pet profile, search local providers, compare reviews/prices, message them, arrange a Meet & Greet, and then book/pay through Rover. Rover provides the marketplace, payments, messaging, support, and various trust/safety mechanisms; it generally  doesn't provide the actual pet care itself .
For sitters, Rover provides customer acquisition, scheduling/booking tools, payments, reviews, and other business-management features.
How Rover makes money
The core model is  transaction fees .
For example, Rover currently says that in its standard U.S. fee structure:
• Pet owners pay an  11% booking fee  at checkout.
• Providers generally pay a  20% service fee , meaning they receive 80% of the booking amount.
• Fees can differ  by market and Rover says some U.S. providers may be participating in different fee programs.
So if a sitter's listed service is $100, Rover's economics are roughly based around taking fees from the transaction rather than charging users a conventional subscription.
Company background
Rover was founded in  2011  and grew into one of the largest online pet-care marketplaces. The broader Rover Group now includes:
• Rover  — dogs and cats, primarily North America and Europe
• Cat in a Flat  — cat-specific care
• Mad Paws  — dog, cat and small-animal care in Australia
An important recent development: Rover was  acquired by Blackstone in February 2024 for approximately $2.3 billion in cash , after which Rover's Nasdaq-listed shares were delisted.
The interesting part
From a  business/technology perspective, Rover is a particularly interesting example of a  local-services marketplace . Its competitive advantage isn't simply the website—it comes from combining:
local supply + consumer demand + reviews/reputation + payments + trust/safety + recurring relationships.
That creates a network effect: more sitters make Rover more useful to pet owners, while more  pet owners make Rover more attractive to sitters.
Rover also has a substantial  trust layer : identity verification/background screening in relevant markets, reviews, Meet & Greets, payment protection, support , and its Rover Guarantee.
If you're asking because you're  evaluating Rover as a business, considering building a competitor, or thinking about becoming a sitter , I  can go much deeper into its  business model, revenue economics, marketplace strategy, technology, competitive moat, weaknesses, and what a Rover-like startup would look like in 2026 .

prompt: What do you know about @roverdotcom on Instagram?
answer:
appears to be the official Instagram account for  Rover , the pet-care marketplace for dog walking, sitting, boarding, and related services. Rover itself has historically linked to that exact Instagram handle from its own website and public materials.
A few things I found:
• Account:  @roverdotcom — branded “Rover | Pet Sitting & Dog Walking.”
• Scale:  A third-party Instagram tracker reported roughly  695K followers  and  5,500+ posts  in July 2026.
• Content:  Primarily pet-focused entertainment, dog/cat stories, pet-care content, and travel/lifestyle material.
• Brand strategy:  Rover has used Instagram for user-generated-content campaigns, contests, promotions, and community engagement for years.
• Important caveat:  The engagement figures from influencer-tracking sites vary and shouldn't be treated as official Instagram analytics. One tracker currently estimates  unusually low engagement relative to the account's follower count.

prompt: What do you know about Rover (https://www.rover.com/)?
answer:
is a large  pet-care marketplace  that connects pet owners with independent sitters, walkers, and other pet-care providers. It was founded in 2011 and is headquartered in Seattle.
What Rover does
For pet parents, Rover is essentially a marketplace for finding someone nearby to care for a dog or cat. Its main services include:
• Boarding  — your pet stays overnight at the sitter's home.
• House sitting  — the sitter stays at your home.
• Doggy day care  — daytime care at the sitter's home.
• Dog walking  — typically 30- or 60-minute walks.
• Drop-in visits  — someone visits your home to feed, play with, walk, or otherwise check on your pet.
• Dog training  — one-on-one in-person training is also offered in some markets.
• Grooming  — Rover is expanding into at-home bathing and grooming.
The basic flow is  search → compare profiles/reviews → message a sitter → optional Meet & Greet → book and pay through Rover . Sitters set their own rates, so prices vary substantially by location, service, demand, and provider.
How Rover makes money
It's a  two-sided marketplace :
Pet owner → Rover → sitter
The owner pays through Rover, and Rover takes a service fee/commission while providing the marketplace, payment infrastructure, marketing, support, and protection programs. For example, Rover currently says U.S. sitters take home  80% of their earnings from each booking , after Rover's fees. There can also be a profile-review fee for people who want to become sitters.
That marketplace model is important: Rover doesn't primarily employ the person walking your dog.  The individual sitter is the service provider , while Rover provides the platform and associated trust/safety infrastructure.
Trust & safety
This is one of the interesting parts of Rover's business model because pet care has a huge  trust problem .
Rover provides things such as:
• Identity/background screening or verification, depending on market
• Verified reviews
• Messaging and photo/video updates
• Meet & Greet functionality
• 24/7 support
• Protection through the  Rover Guarantee  or applicable accident-protection programs
The precise protections vary by country and service, so the guarantee shouldn't be interpreted as equivalent to comprehensive pet insurance.
How big is it?
Rover says the broader Rover Group currently operates across  18 countries , has cared for  12+ million pets , and has facilitated  41 million five-star stays . The group now includes three marketplaces:
• Rover  — primarily dog and cat care in North America and Europe
• Cat in a Flat  — cat-specific care
• Mad Paws  — dog, cat, and small-animal care, particularly in Australia
Ownership changed significantly
One important piece of Rover's corporate history:  Rover used to be publicly traded on Nasdaq under ROVR.
In February 2024,
completed its acquisition of Rover in an all-cash transaction valued at approximately  $2.3 billion . Rover's public shares were delisted, and it became privately held.
So today, it's better thought of as a  Blackstone-owned private marketplace business , rather than a public technology company.
My high-level take
Rover is interesting because it's more than "an app for finding a dog sitter." It's a classic  local-services marketplace  tackling several difficult problems simultaneously:
Supply:  recruit enough quality sitters in each neighborhood ↓ Discovery:  help owners find a suitable provider ↓ Trust:  reviews, verification, screening, Meet & Greets ↓ Transaction:  booking + payment ↓ Retention:  repeat bookings with the same sitter ↓ Expansion:  walks → boarding → daycare → grooming → training
The particularly valuable asset is arguably the  network and trust layer . Once a pet owner finds a sitter they really like, repeat bookings can create strong customer/provider relationships.
There are also obvious marketplace challenges: maintaining consistent quality across independent providers, preventing off-platform transactions, balancing sitter economics with customer prices, dealing with incidents involving animals or homes, and achieving sufficient  liquidity  in every geographic market.
If you're asking because you're  evaluating Rover as a business/company —for example, its business model, revenue economics, competitive moat, valuation, competitors, or whether a Rover-like marketplace could work in another country—I can break that down much more deeply.

Yes. I looked at both the Rover site and recent public information about the company and its social presence.
What Rover is
is a  pet-care marketplace and consumer brand , founded in Seattle in 2011. It connects pet owners with independent pet-care providers, primarily for:
• Dog walking
• Pet sitting / house sitting
• Boarding
• Doggy day care
• Drop-in visits
• Dog training
• Cat care through its broader portfolio
Rover describes itself as a marketplace rather than a traditional pet-care company: the sitter provides the actual care, while Rover provides the discovery, booking, payment, reviews, trust/safety infrastructure, and customer experience.
The interesting business story
Rover has become considerably bigger than just the website many people know.
It went public in 2021 through a SPAC transaction, but in 2023 agreed to be acquired by  Blackstone for approximately $2.3 billion . The transaction subsequently closed, so Rover is now privately held rather than a Nasdaq-listed company.
There has also been a fairly aggressive expansion strategy:
• 2025:  Rover acquired Australia's  Mad Paws , expanding its presence in Australia.
• 2026:  Rover acquired  Meowtel , a  cat-sitting marketplace, giving it a stronger cat-specific offering.
• Rover says it now operates across  16 countries  and has more than  $1 billion in annual sales .
So I would characterize Rover today as a  large, international pet-care marketplace/consumer platform backed by private equity , rather than simply "an app for finding dog walkers."
And @roverdotcom on Instagram
@roverdotcom  is Rover's brand/social-media identity. The broader social  strategy is very clearly  pet-first rather than product-first : cute and funny dogs/cats, relatable pet-parent moments , personality-driven content, and content that makes Rover feel like a pet-loving lifestyle brand rather than a transactional marketplace.
That's an important distinction.
The product is essentially:
"Find and book someone to care for your pet."
But the brand  is closer to:
"Pets are family, and we're the people who understand that."
That positioning is also explicit in Rover's corporate messaging.
One thing I'd  pay attention to
Rover appears to be in an  interesting transition phase  right now.
Historically, the brand was strongly associated with  dogs + dog walking/sitting . More recently, the company has been broadening into  a much larger  pet-care ecosystem , including cats, training and acquisitions such as Meowtel and Mad Paws.

prompt: What do you know about Rover (https://www.rover.com/, @roverdotcom on Instagram)?
answer:
Yes.  Rover  is a major pet-care marketplace and technology company—not a traditional pet-sitting company. It essentially built a two-sided marketplace connecting pet owners with independent pet-care providers.
What Rover is
Rover was founded in  2011 in Seattle  and lets pet parents find, communicate with, book, and pay pet-care providers through its platform. Its core services include:
• 🐕 Dog walking
• 🏠 House sitting
• 🐶 Boarding in a sitter's home
• ☀️ Doggy day care
• 🐾 Drop-in visits
• 🎓 Dog training
• ✂️ Grooming/bathing in some markets
Rover says its broader group now operates in  18 countries , has cared for  12+ million pets , and has facilitated  41 million+ five-star stays .
The important distinction is that  Rover generally doesn't employ the sitter . It operates a marketplace: providers create profiles, set their rates and availability, collect reviews, and build relationships with pet parents, while Rover facilitates discovery, booking, payment, communication and various safety/protection mechanisms.
The business is bigger than just the app
Rover has evolved into a broader  pet-care marketplace/group .
Its current corporate family includes:
• Rover  — dogs and cats, primarily North America and Europe
• Cat in a Flat  — cat-specific care
• Mad Paws  — dog, cat and small-animal care in Australia
And in January 2026 Rover acquired  Meowtel , a U.S. cat-sitting marketplace with 4,000+ providers and more than 125,000 cats served. That's a pretty strong signal that Rover is deliberately expanding beyond its historical "dog walking" identity and deeper into specialized cat care.
Ownership is an interesting part of the story
Rover was once a  public company , trading on Nasdaq under  ROVR . It went public in 2021 via a SPAC transaction.
But that didn't last.
In  February 2024, Blackstone acquired Rover for approximately $2.3 billion , taking it private. Rover's stock was subsequently delisted from Nasdaq.
So today, Rover is a  privately held company backed by Blackstone , rather than a publicly traded startup where you can buy ROVR shares.
Leadership
There's also been a meaningful leadership transition.
Rover co-founder  Aaron Easterly , who had been CEO since the company's founding, became  Executive Chair  in July 2025.  Brent Turner , a longtime Rover executive who had previously been President/COO, became CEO.
That makes the current phase of Rover particularly interesting: it's no longer really a venture-backed startup trying to prove the marketplace concept. It's a large, mature consumer marketplace backed by private equity and looking for additional growth.
How Rover makes money
At a high level, the economics are marketplace economics:
Pet parent → Rover → sitter

is a  pet-care marketplace headquartered in Seattle , connecting pet owners with independent sitters and walkers. The Seattle presence is particularly substantial.
What Rover does
Through its website and app, you can book:
• 🐕  Dog walking
• 🏠  House sitting  — the sitter stays  at your home
• 🐾  Drop-in visits  — feeding, potty breaks , play, etc.
• 🛏️  Dog boarding  — your dog stays  at the sitter's  home
• 🐶  Doggy daycare
• 🐈  Cat sitting / boarding
How big is it in Seattle?
It's quite established locally. As of September 2026, Rover says  12,000+ sitters  offer various services in Seattle. More than  17,700 Seattle pet parents  have booked pet sitting through the platform, while more than  4,900  have booked dog walking.
For pricing, Rover currently reports Seattle averages of approximately:
• $27.75/walk  for dog walking
• $26.75/visit  for  pet sitting/drop -ins
• $23.94/visit  for dog sitting
Those are marketplace  averages; individual sitters  set their own  rates, and Rover  notes that an 11% booking fee  and taxes  apply.
Is  Rover a traditional  pet-care company ?
Not exactly. That's  an important distinction .
Rover is primarily a  platform/marketplace , rather than employing all the people who actually walk or care for the pets. Individual sitters create profiles, choose the services they offer, set their rates and schedules, and communicate with customers through Rover. Rover handles things such as booking, payments, reviews, screening/background checks and customer support.
For  customers, that  gives  you a  lot of choice . The  tradeoff is that the quality of  care depends heavily  on the individual  sitter ,  so  I'd pay close  attention to reviews , repeat clients, experience , cancellation policy and  the meet-and -greet rather than  assuming "Rover" itself  guarantees a particular  level of care .
What about safety ?
Rover says its screened sitters undergo a  third-party background check , bookings are covered by the  Rover Guarantee , and customer support is available 24/7. The guarantee can provide up to  $25,000 in reimbursement for eligible veterinary care , subject to its terms.
I'd still treat  those  protections as a  safety net rather  than  a substitute for  checking  out a sitter  personally.
One interesting Seattle  angle
Rover is genuinely tied to Seattle—not merely a service that happens to operate there. Its Seattle office is listed at  720 Olive Way .

prompt: What do you know about https://www.rover.com/ in United States?
answer:
Yes.
(Rover.com ) is a major U.S. online  marketplace for pet  care , connecting pet owners  with  independent pet sitters , dog walkers, boarders , and other pet -care providers.
What Rover does
Rover was founded in  2011  and operates primarily as a marketplace rather than employing most of the caregivers directly. Pet owners search for providers in their area, review their profiles and reviews, communicate through Rover, and book/pay through the platform.
Services available in the U.S. include:
• Dog boarding  — the pet stays  overnight at the  sitter's home.
• House sitting  — the sitter stays  overnight at the  owner's home.
• Doggy day care  — daytime care at  the sitter's home .
• Dog walking  — typically 30- or  60-minute walks .
• Drop-in visits  — a sitter visits  the pet at  home, generally for  30 or 60  minutes.
• Dog training  and, increasingly,  at-home grooming /bathing  in eligible markets .
How the business  model works
Rover essentially sits  between  pet parents and  independent service providers :
Pet owner → Rover  marketplace → sitter/walker
The provider creates  a profile, chooses  services, sets rates  and availability, and  accepts bookings. Rover  handles the marketplace , payments, messaging, reviews , and various trust /safety mechanisms.
For customers, pricing  isn't a single  Rover-set price :  sitters generally set  their own rates , so prices vary  considerably by location , service, experience, demand , holidays, and additional  pets/services.
Trust  & safety
This is an  important part of  Rover's value proposition . In North America , providers joining Rover  are required to  undergo a background  check, and Rover  provides verified reviews , in -app communication, 24 /7 support, and  protection associated with  bookings.
Rover also advertises  the  Rover Guarantee , including  eligible veterinary-care  reimbursement of up  to  $25,000  for certain situations . That shouldn't be  interpreted as conventional  pet insurance—the  exact coverage, exclusions , and eligibility matter .
How big is  it?
Rover says its  broader group currently  operates across  18 countries , has cared for 12+ million pets , and has facilitated 41 million+ five -star stays/services .
The company has  also been expanding  beyond its original  dog-walking/boarding  marketplace. In  January 2026 , Rover Group announced  its  acquisition of  Meowtel , a U.S . cat-sitting marketplace , strengthening its position  in cat care .
Is Rover legitimate ?
Yes.  Rover is an  established,  mainstream pet-care  marketplace rather than  a questionable booking  site. However, there's  an important distinction :
Rover's platform can  provide screening and  transaction protections , but the individual  sitter is still  the person actually  caring for your  pet.
So if you're  considering using Rover , I'd pay particular  attention to the  individual sitter's  verified reviews, repeat -client history, experience  with your type  of pet, cancellation  policy, availability, and  the Meet & Greet  rather than relying  solely on Rover's  brand.
If you're asking  because you're considering using Rover as  a customer, becoming  a Rover sitter , or studying Rover  as a business /competitor , I can go  much deeper into  the relevant side —including  fees/commission, how  much U.S . sitters actually make , Rover's business model , competitors, or whether  Rover is a  good platform to  work on.

prompt: What do you know about Rover (https://www.rover.com/)?
answer:
is a  pet-care marketplace and technology platform . In simple terms, it connects pet owners with independent people who provide services such as dog walking, pet sitting, boarding, and daycare .
What Rover does
Rover was founded in  2011  and has grown into a large marketplace for dog and cat care. Its current parent organization,  Rover Group , also includes Cat in a Flat and Australia-based Mad Paws. Rover says its marketplaces operate across  18 countries , with more than  12 million pets cared for  and over  41 million five-star stays .
For pet owners, the main services include:
• Boarding  — your pet stays overnight at a sitter's home.
• House sitting  — the sitter stays at your home.
• Doggy daycare  — daytime care at a sitter's home.
• Dog walking  — typically 30- or 60-minute walks.
• Drop-in visits  — a sitter visits your home to feed, play with, and care for your pet.
• Dog training  — in-person training is available in  supported markets.
How the marketplace works
It's essentially a  two-sided marketplace :
Pet parent → Rover → Sitter/walker
A pet owner searches for providers, looks at profiles and reviews, communicates with candidates, and can arrange a Meet & Greet before booking. Payment happens through Rover rather than directly between the two parties. Sitters set their own rates, so pricing varies substantially by location, service, experience, holidays, and additional services.
For providers, Rover is effectively a way to  acquire customers and run a small pet-care business  without having to build their own marketplace, payment infrastructure, scheduling system, review system, etc. Rover explicitly markets this aspect to sitters and walkers.
Trust & safety is a big part of the product
Rover tries to solve one of the biggest problems with peer-to-peer marketplaces:  "Can I trust this stranger with my dog—and potentially my home?"
Its mechanisms include:
• Identity/background screening, depending on market.
• Verified reviews.
• Meet & Greets.
• In-app messaging and photo/video updates.
• 24/7 support.
• Protection/guarantee programs for bookings made through Rover.
Importantly,  Rover isn't itself providing most of the physical pet care . The individual sitter or walker does. That's an important distinction when thinking about its business model, liability, and competitive position.
Why  Rover is interesting as a business
I think the most interesting thing about Rover is that it's  more than an app for finding dog walkers . It's a marketplace attempting to become the infrastructure layer for a fragmented service industry.
It has several reinforcing network effects:
More sitters → more geographic/service coverage → more attractive to pet owners → more bookings → more attractive to sitters.
Reviews and repeat bookings add another layer: once a pet owner finds someone they trust, there's a strong incentive to keep using  that person.
Rover also benefits from the fact that pet care is  recurring rather than purely transactional . Someone might initially use Rover for a vacation boarding stay , then use the same provider for dog walking or daycare later.
The company itself says its platform has millions of services  booked and an average sitter rating of  4.9/5 .
One important caveat
Rover's availability and service mix  varies significantly by country and city . The U.S. experience can be quite different from the European or Australian experience. For example, Rover's U.S. site currently highlights dog walking, boarding, house sitting, daycare, drop-ins,  training, and grooming, while individual markets can offer a different subset.
If you're asking about Rover because you're  evaluating it as a company/business , I can also break down its  business model, revenue/fees, unit economics, competitive moat, history, ownership, and competitors (e.g. Wag, PetBacker, local pet-care businesses) .

prompt: What do you know about https://www.rover.com/ and @roverdotcom on Instagram?
answer:
Yes.
and the Instagram account  @roverdotcom  are associated with  Rover , a large pet-care marketplace.
What Rover is
Rover was founded in  2011  and connects pet owners with independent pet-care providers. Its core services include:
• Dog walking
• Pet sitting / drop-in visits
• House sitting
• Dog boarding
• Doggy day care
• Dog training
• Grooming in some markets
Rover says its marketplace now operates across  18 countries , has facilitated care for  12+ million pets , and has accumulated  41 million+ five-star stays .
The basic model is a marketplace: pet parents find a sitter or walker through Rover, communicate and arrange a Meet & Greet, then book and pay through Rover. Providers are generally independent pet-care businesses rather than Rover employees.
Trust & safety
A major part of Rover's positioning is trust. Rover says providers undergo background checks or identity verification depending on the market, reviews are verified, and bookings receive protections such as the  Rover Guarantee  or accident coverage, along with customer support.
For example, Rover currently advertises up to  $25,000 in reimbursement for eligible veterinary care  under its Rover Guarantee on its U.S. site.
The Instagram account
@roverdotcom  is Rover's consumer-facing social presence. The brand's social-media strategy fits its broader positioning: lots of highly shareable dog/cat content, pet-owner humor, emotional stories, cute animals, and content designed to make Rover feel like a  pet-loving lifestyle brand , rather than simply a transactional booking platform.
That's an important distinction: Rover isn't just selling "30-minute dog walks." Its brand is essentially selling  peace of mind + the emotional relationship people have with their pets .
The bigger company
Rover has expanded beyond the original Rover marketplace. Its current corporate site says  The Rover Group  includes:
• Rover  — dog and cat care, primarily North America and Europe
• Cat in a Flat  — cat-specific care
• Mad Paws  — dog, cat, and small-animal care in Australia
So it's now more of a global pet-care marketplace group than just the website many Americans know as "Rover."
If you're asking because you're  evaluating Rover/@roverdotcom for a brand partnership, influencer campaign, competitive analysis, or trying to understand their Instagram strategy , I can dig much deeper into their  Instagram content, audience, engagement, brand voice, recurring content formats, competitors, and what appears to make their account successful .

Rover was originally a startup founded by  Greg Gottesman, Philip Kimmey, and Aaron Easterly . It grew into the dominant U.S. pet-sitting marketplace and expanded internationally, including through acquisitions such as DogBuddy.
It went public on Nasdaq under  ROVR  in 2021.
But it didn't remain public for long. In  February 2024, Blackstone completed its acquisition of Rover for approximately $2.3 billion , and Rover was delisted from Nasdaq.

The brand

prompt: What do you know about https://www.rover.com/ in Washington?
answer:
If by  Washington  you mean  Washington, D.C. ,
is a pet-care marketplace that connects pet owners with independent sitters and walkers.
What Rover offers in Washington, D.C.
• Dog boarding:  Your dog stays overnight at a sitter's home. Rover currently lists thousands of boarding sitters in D.C.; its site reports an average of about  $54.39/night  as of September 2026.
• House sitting:  A sitter stays at your home and looks after your pet.
• Drop-in visits:  A sitter visits your home to feed, play with, or care for your pet.
• Dog walking
• Doggy day care
• Cat sitting and pet boarding
• Dog training  is also offered through the broader Rover platform.
Rover says sitters are screened with a third-party background check, bookings are paid through the platform, and eligible bookings have protection through the  Rover Guarantee , including up to $25,000 in eligible veterinary-care reimbursement.
Is Rover actually good in D.C.?
There appears to be a  large and active sitter network  in Washington. For example, Rover currently shows sitters in neighborhoods such as Capitol Hill, with profiles displaying verified reviews, repeat clients, experience, and background-check status.
One important distinction:  Rover isn't really a traditional pet-care company where all employees are Rover employees.  You're generally hiring an individual sitter through Rover. That means the quality can vary considerably from one sitter to another.
If you're considering Rover for a  specific dog/cat, boarding dates, or neighborhood in Washington, D.C. , I can also look at the current sitters and tell you  which ones appear most trustworthy and what you should watch out for before booking .

prompt: What do you know about https://www.rover.com/ in United States?
answer:
Yes.
is  a major U.S.  online marketplace for pet care , particularly dog and cat services.
What Rover does
Rover connects pet owners with independent pet-care providers who offer services such as:
• Dog boarding  — your dog stays at the sitter's home.
• House sitting  — the sitter stays at your home with your pet.
• Dog walking
• Drop-in visits
• Doggy day care
• Dog training
• Grooming/bathing  in some markets.
Rover was founded in  2011  and has grown into a large marketplace. The company says its platforms have facilitated  41 million+ 5-star stays , cared for  12+ million pets , and operate across 18 countries.
How the business model works
It's essentially a  two-sided marketplace :
Pet owner → Rover → independent sitter/walker
A pet owner searches for providers in their area, reviews their profiles and ratings, communicates through Rover, can arrange a Meet & Greet, and then pays through the platform. Providers choose their own rates and schedules.
Rover makes money by charging fees on bookings. According to its current U.S. help documentation:
• Pet owners pay an  11% Rover booking fee  at checkout.
• Providers generally pay a  20% service fee , meaning they receive 80% of the booking amount.
• Rover notes that some U.S. providers may be participating in fee pilots,  so the exact economics can vary.
Is Rover legitimate?
Yes.  Rover is an established company rather than a questionable pet-sitting directory. It has a large operating history, substantial user base, verified reviews, identity/background screening processes, in-platform payments and messaging, and customer support.
As an independent signal, Trustpilot currently shows Rover at  4.5/5 from roughly 35,000 reviews , although—as  with any marketplace—individual experiences vary considerably.
The important caveat: Rover isn't the sitter
This is probably the most important thing to understand  about Rover.
Rover is the marketplace/platform; the actual person caring for the animal is generally an independent pet-care provider.  Consequently, the quality of care can vary enormously from one sitter to another.
Rover provides trust/safety mechanisms, verified reviews, screening, messaging, support and its Rover Guarantee, but you still need to evaluate the individual sitter carefully. Rover itself recommends Meet  & Greets before booking.
The Rover Guarantee also isn't equivalent to comprehensive pet insurance. For example, its stated coverage has exclusions  involving illness/pre-existing conditions, certain injuries, Meet & Greets, and bookings made outside Rover.
A significant recent development
Rover Group acquired  Meowtel , a cat -sitting marketplace, in January 2026. Meowtel had more than 4,000 providers and served over 125,000 cats across 8,000+ U.S. cities, so this acquisition  further strengthens Rover's position in cat care.

prompt: What do you know about Rover (https://www.rover.com/)?
answer:
is a  pet-care marketplace  that connects pet owners with independent pet sitters and dog walkers. It was founded in 2011 and has grown into one of the major online pet-care platforms.
What Rover does
For pet owners, Rover lets you find and book local providers for services such as:
• Dog boarding  — your pet stays at the sitter's home.
• House sitting  — the sitter stays at your home.
• Doggy day care
• Dog walking
• Drop-in visits
• In-person dog training  in markets where it's offered.
The basic model is a two-sided marketplace: sitters create profiles, set their own rates and availability, and owners search profiles, reviews and services before booking. Rover handles the booking/payment infrastructure and provides support and booking protection.
How Rover makes money
Rover takes a fee from transactions rather than primarily employing the sitters.
In the U.S., Rover currently says:
• Pet owners pay an  11% booking fee  at checkout.
• Providers generally pay a  20% service fee , meaning they take home 80% of their booking revenue.
• There are some market- and provider-specific exceptions, including different arrangements in California and certain pilot programs.
So, economically, Rover is essentially a  marketplace + payments + trust/safety layer  sitting between pet owners and local service providers.
Trust & safety
This is a particularly important part of the proposition. Rover uses identity verification/screening, reviews,  in-app messaging, Meet & Greets, customer support and its  Rover Guarantee/booking protection  to reduce the perceived risk of leaving a pet with a stranger.
That trust layer is arguably one of Rover's biggest competitive advantages: the product isn't just "find a dog sitter"; it's  find someone, evaluate them, communicate with them, pay them, and have some protection if something goes wrong.
Company / ownership
There's an interesting corporate-history point: Rover used  to be a  publicly traded company on Nasdaq . In February 2024, private-equity funds affiliated with  Blackstone  completed an approximately  $2.3 billion acquisition  of Rover. Rover's public stock  was subsequently delisted.
Rover now describes itself as part of the  Rover Group , alongside  Cat in a Flat  and  Mad Paws , with operations spanning multiple markets. Its current site says the group operates in 18 countries and has facilitated care for 12+ million pets.
One important limitation
Rover isn't really a  traditional "pet-care company" in the sense of owning kennels or employing a huge workforce of sitters. It's much closer to  Airbnb/Uber-style marketplace infrastructure for pet care : the individual provider supplies the service, while Rover supplies demand, discovery, reputation, payments, software and safety mechanisms.
If you're  asking because you're  evaluating Rover as a business, competitor, investment/acquisition target, or thinking about building something similar , I can also break down its  business model, unit economics, marketplace dynamics, competitive moat, weaknesses, and what I think Rover's biggest opportunities are in 2026 .

answer:
If you mean  Rover (@roverdotcom) , the pet-care brand, here’s the short version:
• Rover is a pet-care marketplace  founded in 2011 that connects pet owners with local sitters, dog walkers, boarding  providers, and trainers.
• Its core services include  dog walking, drop-in visits, boarding, house sitting, doggy day care, and training ; offerings vary by market.
• Rover operates as a  two-sided marketplace : pet parents book through the platform, while independent pet-care providers set their  own rates and schedules.
• The company emphasizes trust mechanisms such as  background checks/identity verification, verified reviews, Meet & Greets, 24/7 support, and protection through the Rover Guarantee or applicable coverage .
• Today , Rover says its broader  Rover Group  spans 18 countries and includes  Rover, Cat in a Flat, and Mad Paws . It reports 12+ million pets cared for and 41 million 5-star bookings.
What about @roverdotcom specifically?
The Instagram account is the brand's main social presence,  Rover | Pet Sitting & Dog Walking . A third-party Instagram analytics page currently reports roughly  695K followers  and more than  5,500 posts , with content centered on pets, pet owners, and travel/lifestyle.
What makes Rover interesting from a  brand/marketing perspective  is that it's not really selling "dog walking" as its emotional product. Its marketing is much more about  the relationship between people and their pets —using funny, cute, highly shareable pet content to build affinity, while Rover sits in the background as the trusted solution when someone needs care.

prompt: What do you know about Rover (https://www.rover.com/, @roverdotcom on Instagram)?
answer:
is a major  pet-care marketplace and technology platform —essentially a way for pet owners to find and book independent pet  sitters, dog walkers, and related services.
What Rover does
Rover was founded in  2011  and connects pet parents with local care providers. Its core services include:
• Dog walking
• Pet boarding  — the pet stays at the sitter's home
• House sitting  — the sitter stays at the owner's home
• Drop-in visits
• Doggy day care
• Dog training
• Grooming  in some markets
The basic model is marketplace-driven: sitters create profiles, set their rates and availability, collect reviews, and pet owners search, message, arrange a Meet & Greet, and pay through Rover.
It's bigger than just "dog walking"
Rover says its platform now operates across  18 countries , with  12+ million pets cared for  and  41 million 5-star stays/bookings . The broader Rover Group also includes  Cat in a Flat  and  Mad Paws , extending its reach into cat care and Australia.
For sitters, Rover is effectively a  customer-acquisition + payments + scheduling + trust/safety platform . Providers can run their own pet-care business through the marketplace rather than being Rover employees. Rover says sitters control their rates and schedules.
The trust/safety proposition
A big part of Rover's value proposition is reducing the uncertainty of hiring a stranger to care for your pet. Depending on the market, Rover provides things such as:
• Identity verification/background checks
• Verified reviews
• In-app messaging and photo sharing
• Meet & Greets
• 24/7 support
• Booking protection / the  Rover Guarantee
For example, in the U.S., Rover currently advertises the Rover Guarantee with up to  $25,000 reimbursement for eligible veterinary care .
The business model
At  a high level, Rover is a  two-sided marketplace :
Pet owner → Rover → sitter
The owner gets convenience, discovery, reviews, payments and some protections; the sitter gets access  to potential customers and business-management infrastructure. Rover makes money by taking fees associated with bookings rather than operating a fleet of employed dog  walkers.
That's an important distinction:  Rover generally isn't the company sending its own employees to walk your dog.  It's facilitating transactions between pet owners and independent providers.
And  the Instagram account
The  @roverdotcom  account is Rover's consumer-facing social presence. The brand is particularly well suited to social media because its marketing naturally revolves  around  cute/relatable pet content, pet-parent culture, and the emotional idea that pets are family , rather than simply advertising a transactional service. Rover explicitly  frames its brand around that "pets are family" positioning.
If you're asking because you're  researching Rover as a company/brand  rather than simply wondering  what the service is, I can also dig into its  ownership, leadership, revenue/business model, competitors, marketing strategy, Instagram presence, and how Rover compares with Wag and other pet-care marketplaces .

prompt: What do you know about https://www.rover.com/ in Washington?
answer:
If by  Washington  you mean  Washington, D.C. ,
is a pet-care marketplace where people can find and book local pet sitters and dog walkers.
In D.C., Rover currently offers:
• Dog walking  — typically 30-minute neighborhood walks.
• Drop-in visits  — someone comes to your home to feed, play with, or care for your pet.
• House sitting  — the sitter stays at your home.
• Dog/cat boarding  — your pet stays at the sitter's home.
• Doggy day care .
In D.C., Rover currently offers:
What it looks like in Washington, D.C.
Rover says that, as of September 2026, there are  thousands of sitters/walkers listed in the D.C. area . Its current published averages are about  $22.20 per dog walk  and  $23.54 per pet-sitting visit , although individual prices vary considerably. Rover also adds an  11% booking fee plus taxes  according to its D.C. listings.
Rover says sitters undergo a  third-party background check , bookings are handled through its platform, and eligible bookings are covered by its Rover Guarantee, including up to  $25,000 in eligible veterinary-care reimbursement .
One thing I'd distinguish:  Rover isn't itself a traditional local pet-sitting company . It's a marketplace connecting you with independent sitters. That means the quality can vary substantially from one sitter to another, so reviews, repeat clients, experience, availability, and a meet-and-greet are worth paying attention to.
If you're asking because you're considering  using Rover in Washington, D.C. , I can also compare it with local independent pet-care businesses and tell you  whether Rover is a good deal, what to watch out for, and which option I'd choose .

prompt: What do you know about https://www.rover.com/ in United States?
answer:
Yes.
(Rover.com) is a major U.S. online marketplace for  dog and cat care , connecting pet owners with independent pet sitters, walkers, and other pet-care providers.
What Rover does
Rover was founded in  2011  and operates as a marketplace rather than employing the individual sitters directly. In the U.S., pet owners can use it for:
• Dog boarding  — your dog stays  overnight at a sitter's home.
• House sitting  — the sitter stays at your home with your pet.
• Doggy day care  — daytime care at a sitter's home.
• Dog walking  — typically 30- or 60-minute walks.
• Drop-in visits  —  a sitter visits your home, generally for 30 or 60 minutes.
• Dog training  — in-person training with participating trainers.
• Grooming  — Rover has also been expanding into at-home grooming/bathing.
How the marketplace works
A typical customer journey is:
Enter your location, dates, pet information and  desired service.
Browse local sitters and walkers.
Compare profiles, prices, availability and reviews.
Message prospective sitters.
Arrange a  Meet & Greet .
Book and  pay through Rover.
Rover recommends contacting multiple providers and meeting them before booking, particularly for a first-time sitter.
An important point is that  sitters set their own rates , so pricing varies substantially by location, service, experience, number of pets and sometimes holidays/add-ons.
Trust & safety
Rover has several mechanisms intended to reduce the risk of using a stranger to care for your pet:
• Background screening/identity verification for providers, depending on the market  and service.
• Verified customer reviews.
• In-platform messaging and payments.
• 24/7 customer support.
• The  Rover Guarantee/RoverProtect  programs for eligible situations and expenses.
That said, I'd distinguish  "Rover has safety mechanisms"  from  "every Rover sitter is equally reliable."  The individual sitter matters enormously. Reviews, repeat customers, experience with your type of pet, communication and a Meet & Greet are worth evaluating carefully.
It's also a gig-work platform
For providers, Rover is effectively a way to operate a small pet-care business through an established marketplace. Rover explicitly says its sitters and walkers are  independent contractors, not Rover employees .
This creates an interesting two-sided business:
Pet owners → Rover → independent pet-care providers
Rover  handles the marketplace, discovery, booking/payment infrastructure, reviews, trust mechanisms and customer support, while the sitter supplies the actual care.
Scale
Rover says its broader group has  facilitated  41+ million five-star stays , cared for  12+ million pets , and operates across  18 countries . The Rover brand itself focuses on dog and cat care in North  America and Europe.
If you're researching Rover for business reasons
I can also go deeper into  Rover's U.S. business model , including  how Rover makes money, sitter fees/commission, customer fees, estimated economics per booking, competitors (Wag, local kennels, etc.), its history/acquisitions, ownership, and whether a similar Rover-style marketplace could work in another country .

prompt: What do you know about https://www.rover.com/?
answer:
is a  pet-care marketplace  that connects pet owners with  independent sitters and other pet-care providers. It was founded in 2011 and is now part of the  Rover Group , which also includes Cat in a Flat and Mad Paws.
What Rover offers
Depending on the market, you can book:
• Dog/cat boarding  — your pet stays at  the sitter's home.
• House sitting  — the sitter stays at your home.
• Doggy day care
• Dog walking
• Drop-in visits  — typically 30- or 60-minute visits.
• Dog training
• Grooming  in some markets.
The basic model is similar to Airbnb/Uber: Rover provides the  marketplace, profiles, reviews, messaging, booking and payment infrastructure , while individual sitters provide the actual care. Sitters generally set their own rates.
Trust & safety
Rover puts considerable emphasis on trust signals. It says sitters undergo identity verification/background screening depending on the country,  and users can see reviews, repeat-client information and other profile details. It also recommends doing a  Meet & Greet  before booking.
Bookings also come with Rover's protection program. In the U.S., for example, Rover currently advertises the  Rover Guarantee with up to $25,000 reimbursement for eligible veterinary care , plus 24/7 support. The exact protection and limits vary by market.
Scale
Rover says its marketplace operates  in  18 countries , has cared for  12+ million pets , and has accumulated  41 million five-star stays . Those are Rover's own reported figures, so I'd treat them as company-reported rather than independently audited statistics.
The important caveat
Rover  isn't itself the pet-care provider  in the usual sense. You're hiring an individual sitter through Rover.  That means the quality can vary enormously from one sitter to another. The platform's reviews, screening, Meet & Greet and protection mechanisms reduce some risk, but they  don't make every sitter equivalent to a professional kennel, veterinary facility, or established pet-care business.
Also,  availability and services are highly location-dependent . For example, the version of Rover I can currently access is showing European markets; Rover's parent company says its different brands/platforms cover North America, Europe and  Australia.
If you're asking because you're considering  using Rover, becoming a Rover sitter, or evaluating Rover as a business/company , I can  go considerably deeper—for example,  how Rover makes money, its fees/commission structure, pros & cons for sitters, or whether it's available/useful in Bali/Indonesia .

prompt: What do you know about Rover (https://www.rover.com/)?
answer:
is a  two-sided online marketplace for pet care , best known for connecting pet owners with  independent sitters and walkers. It was founded in 2011 and operates primarily across North America and Europe.
What Rover actually does
For pet parents, Rover lets you search local providers, compare profiles and reviews, message them, arrange a Meet & Greet, and then book/pay through the platform. Services include:
• Boarding  — pet stays overnight at the sitter's home
• House sitting  — sitter stays at the owner's home
• Doggy day care
• Dog walking
• Drop-in visits
• Dog training  — a newer service for credentialed trainers
• Grooming  — available in some markets
The interesting part is that Rover generally  doesn't employ the caregivers . It provides the marketplace, discovery, payments, messaging, trust/safety infrastructure and customer support while sitters operate their own pet-care businesses. Rover explicitly markets itself as helping sitters "launch, grow, and maintain" their businesses.
The trust layer is a big part of the product
Rover's core problem isn't simply "find someone to walk my dog." It's  "How do I trust a stranger with my pet and potentially my home?"
So the platform has built around:
• Identity/background screening,  depending on market
• Verified reviews
• Profiles showing experience and care preferences
• Meet & Greets
• In-app communication and photo updates
• 24/7 support
• Booking protection /Rover Guarantee, with terms varying by market
Rover currently says its network has cared for  12+ million pets , with  41 million 5-star stays , across  18 countries .
It's becoming more than "dog sitting"
There's an interesting strategic evolution  happening.
Rover has expanded beyond its original dog-walking/boarding marketplace into adjacent pet services. In 202 6, for example, it launched its dog-training offering nationally in the U.S., with credentialed trainers.
And in January 2026, Rover Group acquired  Meowtel , a cat-sitting marketplace, expanding its focus on cat-specific care. The broader Rover Group also includes  Cat in a Flat  and  Mad Paws .
So I'd think of Rover less as "an app for finding dog walkers" and more as:
A marketplace infrastructure layer for the fragmented pet-care economy.
That's potentially the most interesting thing about the company.
The business-model angle
The marketplace has  a classic network-effect structure:
Pet owners → demand → sitters → supply → more choice → better marketplace → more pet owners
Rover gets value from facilitating transactions rather than having to own physical kennels, employ thousands of walkers, or  operate veterinary clinics itself.
That also creates the classic marketplace challenges: maintaining supply quality, building trust, preventing transactions from moving off-platform, balancing  sitter economics with customer prices, and achieving enough density in each geographic market.
If you're asking because you're  evaluating Rover as a company/business model, considering building something similar, researching its economics, or wondering whether Rover is a good service to use , I  can go considerably deeper into whichever angle you're interested in.

• 🏠 House sitting
• 🛏️ In-home boarding
• ☀️ Doggy daycare
• 🚪 Drop-in visits
• 🐈 Cat  sitting
• 🎓  Dog training
• ✂️ Grooming, depending on market
Rover says its network has cared for  12+ million pets , with  41 million+ five-star stays , operates across  18 countries , and has an average sitter rating of  4.9/5 .
How the business works
The basic model is a two-sided marketplace:
Pet parent → searches providers → Meet & Greet → books/pays through Rover → sitter provides care → review
Rover handles discovery, payments, messaging, reviews, customer support and various safety/protection mechanisms. Providers set up profiles, services, rates, availability and pet preferences.
Importantly, the people actually caring for the animals are generally the individual providers—not Rover employees. Rover is essentially the technology/marketplace layer connecting the two sides.
Trust & safety
This is a major part of Rover's value proposition. Rover says it provides background checks for sitters and dog walkers, verified reviews, identity verification, on-platform messaging, secure payments, 24/7 support and the  Rover Guarantee  for eligible incidents.
Rover strongly encourages keeping both  communication and payment on its platform , partly because going off-platform can mean losing protections such as the Rover Guarantee and support.
The economics
Rover takes a cut of transactions rather than charging pet parents simply to browse the marketplace. The exact fee structure varies substantially by country and sometimes by provider/account.
For example, Rover's current U.S. help documentation says providers take home  80% of their earnings  on bookings, after Rover's service fee.
That's an important distinction if you're evaluating Rover as a  business/marketplace : its revenue is fundamentally tied to the volume and value of pet-care transactions flowing through the platform.
Who owns Rover?
This is an interesting part of the company's story.
Rover was formerly a publicly traded company,  Rover Group, Inc. (NASDAQ: ROVR) . In February 2024,
completed its acquisition of Rover in an all-cash deal valued at approximately  $2.3 billion . Rover's public shares were subsequently delisted, and Rover became privately held.
So today, Rover is a  Blackstone-owned private company , rather than a publicly traded startup.
The broader Rover Group
Rover has also expanded beyond the original U.S.-focused dog-sitting marketplace. Its current corporate group includes:
• Rover  — dog and cat care, primarily North America and Europe
• Cat in a Flat  — cat-specific care
• Mad Paws  — dog, cat and small-animal care, particularly Australia
Rover says the group operates across  18 countries .
Instagram / brand
The @roverdotcom  Instagram account fits with Rover's broader consumer brand: it's not just advertising "book a dog sitter." Rover  has built a fairly recognizable  pet-lifestyle/media brand  around dogs, cats, pet-parent culture, educational content, humor and shareable pet  content.
That brand layer is strategically useful because pet care is a trust-heavy category: people aren't merely choosing a service provider—they're entrusting someone with a  family member.

prompt: What do you know about https://www.rover.com/ in Washington?
answer:
If by  Washington  you mean  Washington, D.C . , Rover is a  large marketplace for  booking local pet -care providers rather  than a traditional  pet-care company  with its own  employees.
What Rover offers in Washington, D.C.
You can use the platform to find individuals offering:
• Dog walking
• Drop-in visits  at your home
• House sitting
• Dog boarding  at the sitter's  home
• Doggy day care
• Cat sitting/pet  sitting
Rover says its  D.C. sitters  are screened with  third-party background  checks, have reviews  from other pet  owners, and bookings  include its Rover  Guarantee and 24 /7 support.
How big is it locally?
It's quite established in D.C. Rover currently reports  12,500+ pet parents  having booked pet sitting in Washington, D.C., with thousands of local sitters listed. For example, its current D.C. dog-sitting page reports more than  16,000 sitters  offering that service.
Pricing varies considerably because individual sitters set their own rates. As of September 2026, Rover reports an average of roughly  $22–$24 per visit  for D.C. dog/pet sitting, with an  11% booking fee plus taxes .
Is Rover trustworthy?
Generally, yes—but the individual sitter matters enormously.  Rover gives you the marketplace infrastructure: profiles, reviews, background checks, payment processing, customer support, and protection. But you're ultimately choosing an independent pet sitter/walker.
I'd pay particular attention to:
• Number of  completed/repeat bookings , not just star  rating
• Detailed recent reviews
• Whether they've cared  for pets with  similar needs
• Their cancellation policy
• Response time and  communication
• A  Meet & Greet  before the first  booking
• Exactly what is  and isn't covered  by Rover's guarantee /insurance
If you're asking because you're considering  using Rover in Washington, D.C. , I can also look at the  best-rated Rover sitters in a particular D.C. neighborhood , compare their prices/reviews, and tell you which ones I'd shortlist.

prompt: What do you know about https://www.rover.com/ in United States?
answer:
Yes.
is a major U.S.  online marketplace for pet care , primarily connecting dog/cat owners with  independent pet sitters, walkers, boarders, and other pet-care providers.
What Rover does
Rover was founded in  2011  and operates as a marketplace rather than directly employing most of the people providing the care. Pet owners search profiles, compare reviews/prices, communicate with providers, and book/pay through Rover.
Its main U.S. services include:
• Dog boarding  — the pet stays overnight at the sitter's home.
• House sitting  —  the sitter stays at the owner's home.
• Doggy day care  — daytime care at the sitter's home.
• Dog walking  — typically 30- or 60-minute walks.
• Drop-in visits  — a sitter visits the pet at home.
• Dog training  — Rover launched private, in-person training with credentialed trainers across the U.S. in 2026.
• Grooming  — Rover is also expanding into at-home bathing/grooming.
How the marketplace works
A typical customer journey is:
Search → compare sitters → read reviews → Meet & Greet → book/pay through Rover → receive updates/photos.
Providers set their own rates and availability, so prices vary substantially by city, service, experience, holidays, number of pets, and additional requirements.
Rover also provides marketplace infrastructure such as:
• Profile and review system
• Messaging and photo sharing
• Online payments
• Identity/background screening
• 24/ 7 support
• Booking protection/Rover Guarantee
• Tools for sitters to manage their schedules and business
How big is it?
Rover describes  itself as a large global pet-care marketplace. Its current corporate information says the broader Rover Group operates in  18 countries , has cared for  12+ million pets , and has facilitated  41 million 5-star stays .
The company is now part of  Rover Group , which also includes  Cat in a Flat  and  Mad Paws .
If you're evaluating Rover as a business
What's particularly interesting about Rover is that it is essentially a  two-sided marketplace :
Pet owners ↔ Rover platform ↔ independent pet-care providers
Rover  can therefore generate value without owning boarding facilities or employing thousands of sitters directly. Its competitive advantages are largely the  local supply network, reviews/reputation, trust & safety infrastructure, payments, customer acquisition, and repeat bookings .
For sitters, Rover says they can set their own schedule and prices and withdraw payment  after completing services.
For pet owners, the biggest value proposition is  convenience + local choice + trust signals , rather than simply finding  the cheapest sitter.
If you're asking because you're considering  using Rover, becoming a Rover sitter, investing/researching the company, or building a similar marketplace ,  I can go much deeper—for example, into  Rover's U.S. business model, fees/commission structure, estimated revenue, competitors (Wag, PetBacker, local kennels), or how the platform works technically.

prompt: What do you know about Rover (https://www.rover.com/)?
answer:
is essentially a  two-sided marketplace for pet care , best known for connecting pet owners with independent dog walkers and pet sitters.
What Rover does
For pet owners, Rover lets you find and book local providers for:
• Dog walking
• Drop-in visits  — someone visits your home to feed, play with, or care for your pet
• House sitting  — the sitter stays in your home
• Boarding  — your pet stays at the sitter's home
• Doggy day care
• Dog training
• At-home bathing/grooming  is also now being offered in some markets.
The basic flow is marketplace-style: search → compare provider profiles/reviews → message them → optionally have a Meet & Greet → book and pay through Rover. Providers set their own prices and availability.
The business model
The interesting part of Rover is that it isn't primarily a traditional pet-care company.  It's a platform connecting supply and demand.
On one side:
Pet owners who need trustworthy, convenient care.
On the other:
Individuals/professionals who want to earn money caring for pets.
Rover handles much of the marketplace infrastructure: discovery, profiles, reviews, payments, messaging, scheduling, customer support and safety mechanisms.
Rover says sitters are  independent contractors rather than Rover employees , and providers set their own schedules and rates.
For providers, Rover currently says they take home  80% of their booking earnings , with the remainder supporting the platform's services, marketing, Rover Guarantee, and support. There can also be a profile-review fee to join, varying by location.
Trust & safety is a major part of the product
This is particularly important because Rover is essentially asking you to trust a stranger with  your pet—and sometimes your home .
Rover uses things such as:
• Background checks
• Verified reviews
• Provider profiles and repeat-client  information
• In-platform messaging and payments
• Meet & Greets
• 24/7 support
• Its  Rover Guarantee , which currently includes up to  $25,000 in reimbursement for eligible veterinary care.
That trust layer is arguably one of Rover's biggest competitive advantages over simply finding someone through Craigslist, Facebook, Google, or word of mouth.
Why Rover is interesting
If you're asking about Rover because you're  studying the company/business , I think the really interesting thing is the marketplace architecture.
It combines:
Local marketplace + reputation system + payments + scheduling + insurance/guarantee + mobile app + recurring services.
And pet care has some unusually strong marketplace characteristics:
• Highly fragmented supply
• Recurring demand
• Local transactions
• Strong emotional attachment
• Trust is extremely important
• Providers can potentially become repeat providers
• A customer who needs a dog walker may later need boarding, house sitting, etc.
Rover explicitly leans into that cross-selling: the same provider can offer multiple services, allowing a relationship that starts with a walk to turn into boarding or house sitting.
One caveat:  Rover is primarily oriented around dogs and cats , although individual providers may have experience with other animals.
If your interest is  Rover as a company rather than simply as a pet-sitting website , I can  also break down its  history, ownership/public-company status, revenue/business model, competitors (Wag, PetBacker, etc.), unit economics, moat, and how the marketplace actually works .
