prompt: What do you know about https://www.rover.com/ and @roverdotcom on Instagram?
answer:
Yes. I looked into both the website and the Instagram account.
What Rover is
is a major pet-care marketplace founded in 2011 and headquartered in Seattle. It connects dog and cat owners with independent pet-care providers. Its core services currently include:
• Dog walking
• Boarding in a sitter's home
• House sitting
• Drop-in visits
• Doggy day care
• Dog training
Rover describes itself as a marketplace rather than a traditional pet-care company: sitters and walkers create profiles, set their own rates, receive reviews, and customers book and pay through the platform.
A little business history
Rover has become quite a large company. It went public on Nasdaq in 2021 through a SPAC transaction, under the ticker ROVR.
Then in 2023,
agreed to acquire Rover for approximately  $2.3 billion . The acquisition subsequently closed, taking Rover private.
It has also been expanding internationally through acquisitions , including DogBuddy and, more recently, Gudog and Cat in a Flat.
What about @roverdotcom?
The Instagram handle  @roverdotcom  is Rover's branded social-media presence. The overall brand positioning is very much  “pet love + entertaining pet content + practical pet-parent advice,”  rather than simply advertising its booking marketplace.
That's consistent with Rover's broader content strategy. The company has historically invested heavily in  editorial/content marketing through  The Dog People , alongside its core marketplace.
One useful distinction:  Rover's Instagram isn't the same thing as Rover's marketplace.  The marketplace is the transactional product; Instagram is primarily a brand/community/content channel designed to make Rover culturally relevant to pet owners.
If you're asking because you're considering  working with Rover, pitching them, analyzing their Instagram strategy, or trying to understand whether @roverdotcom is a good account/brand partner , I can go  much deeper—for example, I can analyze their  Instagram content, audience, engagement, brand voice, competitors, influencer strategy, and what kinds of collaborations they appear to pursue.

prompt: What do you know about Rover (https://www.rover.com/, @roverdotcom on Instagram)?
answer:
Yes.
is a major pet-care marketplace and technology company —essentially a platform that connects pet parents with  independent pet sitters, dog walkers, and other pet-care providers.
What Rover does
Rover was founded in  2011  and operates primarily as a two-sided marketplace:
• Pet parents  can find and book local providers for dog/cat boarding, house sitting, dog walking, drop-in visits, doggy day care, and , increasingly, dog training.
• Sitters and walkers  create profiles, set their own rates, describe their experience/services, receive reviews, communicate with clients, and get paid through the platform.
• Rover handles much of the marketplace infrastructure: discovery, booking, payments, messaging, reviews, support, and various safety mechanisms.
It's therefore closer to  Airbnb/Uber for pet care  than to a traditional pet-sitting agency: the people providing the actual care are generally independent providers rather than Rover employees.
Its scale
Rover says its broader Rover Group currently operates in  18 countries , has facilitated care for  12+ million pets , and has accumulated  41 million+ five-star stays . The group now includes  Rover, Cat in a Flat, and Mad Paws .
Trust & safety is a big part of the proposition
One of Rover's biggest selling points is reducing the anxiety involved in handing your pet—and sometimes your home—to a stranger.
The platform says it provides:
• Background checks for sitters/walkers
• Verified reviews
• Meet & Greets before bookings
• In-app communication and photo sharing
• Cashless payments
• 24/7 support
• Reservation protection
• The  Rover Guarantee , which can provide reimbursement for certain eligible losses/ veterinary expenses.
Importantly,  the Rover Guarantee is not pet insurance . Rover explicitly distinguishes the two.
The business model
The interesting thing about Rover is that it doesn't primarily need to employ thousands of sitters itself. It operates  the  marketplace layer  and takes fees associated with transactions.
That creates a potentially attractive model:
Pet parent → Rover marketplace → independent sitter → pet care
The more pet owners use Rover, the more attractive it can become to sitters; the more quality sitters are available, the more useful Rover becomes to pet owners. That's the classic  two-sided network-effect marketplace  dynamic.
There is also an interesting retention loop: a customer might initially use Rover for a weekend boarding stay, then use the same provider for  recurring walks or future trips. Rover explicitly encourages this kind of repeat relationship.
And @roverdotcom
The Instagram account you mentioned is the  social-facing side of that brand. Rover's consumer brand is very deliberately  emotion-first : cute animals, pet-parent identity, humor, relatable pet behavior , and the idea that pets are family.
That's strategically useful because Rover isn't really selling "a booking platform." It's selling  peace of mind around something people are emotionally attached to .
If you're asking because you're  researching Rover as a company/brand —for example, its  business model, marketing strategy, Instagram/content strategy, competitors, growth, financials, or why its brand works — I can go much deeper into that.

prompt: What do you know about https://www.rover.com/ in United States?
answer:
is a major  U.S.-focused online marketplace for pet care , connecting pet owners with independent pet sitters, dog walkers, trainers, and related providers.
What Rover does
Rover essentially acts as a marketplace between  pet parents and local caregivers . In the U.S., its main services include:
• Dog boarding  — your dog or cat stays overnight at a sitter's home.
• House sitting  — the sitter stays at your home with your pets.
• Doggy day care  — daytime care at a sitter's home.
• Dog walking  — typically 30- or 60-minute walks.
• Drop-in visits  — a sitter visits your home to feed, play with, and care for your pet.
• Dog training  — one-on-one training with credentialed trainers.
• At-home grooming/bathing  is also being offered as a newer service.
The basic process is  search → review sitter profiles → communicate/Meet & Greet → book and pay through Rover . Sitters set their own rates and availability.
How big is it?
Rover was founded in  2011  and says the broader Rover Group currently operates in  18 countries , with  12+ million pets cared for ,  41 million five-star stays , and an average sitter rating of  4.9/5 . The group also includes Cat in a Flat and Mad Paws.
One important corporate detail:  Rover is no longer a publicly traded company.  Private-equity funds affiliated with  Blackstone  completed their approximately  $2.3 billion acquisition of Rover in February 2024 , after which Rover's Nasdaq listing was terminated.
Trust and safety
Rover has built several protections into the marketplace:
• Background checks for pet-care providers.
• Verified reviews.
• In-person Meet & Greets.
• Secure payments through the platform.
• 24/7 customer support.
• The  Rover Guarantee , which Rover says can provide up to  $25,000 in reimbursement for eligible veterinary care .
That said, an important distinction is that  Rover is a marketplace, not a traditional pet-care employer . The individual sitter is the person actually providing the care, so the quality can vary considerably from one provider to another. Rover itself recommends looking at reviews, experience, repeat-client statistics, trust badges, and doing a Meet & Greet.
If you're looking at Rover as a business
It's an interesting company because its model is essentially:
Pet owner → Rover marketplace → independent sitter → Rover takes a platform fee
The value proposition is that Rover handles discovery, profiles/reviews, messaging, payments, trust/safety infrastructure and marketplace demand, while sitters supply the actual service.
For a sitter, Rover promotes the ability to  set your own prices, schedule, services and pet preferences , while using Rover to find customers.
So if you're asking because you're considering  using Rover, becoming a Rover sitter, investing in/competing with Rover, or building a similar marketplace , I can go much deeper—for example, I can break down  Rover's U.S. business model, fees, estimated revenue/economics, competitors (Wag, PetBacker, etc.), customer acquisition strategy, and how profitable it is for a typical sitter.

prompt: What do you know about https://www.rover.com/?
answer:
is a large online marketplace for  pet-care services , essentially matching pet owners with independent pet sitters, walkers, boarders, and other providers.
The core services include  dog/cat boarding in a sitter’s home, house sitting in the owner’s home, dog walking, drop-in visits, doggy daycare, and—in some markets—training and grooming . Owners search by location and dates, compare profiles, rates, reviews and experience, optionally arrange a Meet & Greet, and then book/pay through Rover.
How the business model works
Rover is a  two-sided marketplace  rather than a traditional pet-care company employing all the sitters. Providers generally run their own pet-care businesses and set their own rates. Rover supplies the marketplace, payments, messaging, reviews, customer acquisition and safety/support infrastructure.
In the U.S., Rover currently says pet owners generally pay an  11% booking fee , while pet-care providers generally pay a  20% service fee , meaning the provider keeps about 80% of the listed earnings. There are exceptions and pilot programs, and fees vary by geography. Rover also currently charges prospective U.S. providers a  $49–$79 profile-review fee , depending on location.
For example, very roughly, if a sitter's service is priced at  $50 , Rover's standard 20% provider fee would leave the sitter with about  $40 , while the customer may also have a booking fee added at checkout. Exact totals depend on the booking and market.
Trust and safety
This is an important part of Rover's value proposition because you're potentially giving a stranger access to your pet and/or home. Rover says providers joining the platform undergo background checks; profiles have verified reviews and other trust signals; bookings include 24/7 support and reservation protection; and the  Rover Guarantee  can reimburse up to  $25,000 in eligible veterinary expenses  in qualifying situations. Rover also encourages owners to conduct an in-person Meet & Greet before hiring someone.
It's worth understanding that the Rover Guarantee isn't the same thing as ordinary pet insurance, and using a marketplace doesn't eliminate the need to vet an individual sitter carefully.
How big is Rover?
Rover was founded in  2011  and is based in Seattle. Rover says its broader group now operates across  18 countries , has cared for  12+ million pets , and has accumulated  41 million five-star stays  across its marketplaces. The Rover Group also includes  Cat in a Flat  and  Mad Paws .
There's also an interesting ownership story. Rover used to be publicly traded on Nasdaq, but private-equity firm
acquired it in  February 2024 for approximately $2.3 billion , after which Rover became privately held and its shares were delisted.
The interesting part: the marketplace economics
Rover is basically an  “Airbnb/Uber-style marketplace for pet care.”  Its main asset isn't kennels or a huge employed workforce; it's the network connecting local pet owners and providers.
That creates a classic marketplace flywheel:
more sitters → more availability/choice → more pet owners → more bookings → better earning opportunity → more sitters.
It also creates an obvious tension: once an owner and sitter know and trust each other, they could theoretically transact directly and avoid marketplace fees. Rover explicitly requires relationships originating through Rover to keep subsequent bookings on the platform under its terms. Its pitch for staying on-platform is payments, support, safety tools and Rover Guarantee coverage.
So if you're studying Rover because you're thinking about  using it , I can break down whether it's worth the fees and what to look for in a sitter. If you're looking at it from a  business/startup perspective , I can instead dissect Rover's business model, unit economics, network effects, competitive moat, and how difficult it would be to build a Rover competitor.

prompt: What do you know about Rover (https://www.rover.com/)?
answer:
is a two-sided marketplace for pet care: it connects pet owners with independent sitters, dog walkers, boarders, and trainers. Think of it roughly as an Airbnb/Uber-style marketplace, except the  transaction is pet care rather than accommodation or transportation.
Rover was founded in Seattle in 2011 and has grown into a major pet-services marketplace. It was publicly traded for several years,  but in February 2024 private-equity funds affiliated with
completed an acquisition valued at about  $2.3 billion , taking Rover private.
What Rover actually sells
Rover itself generally isn't employing the  person who takes care of your pet. Instead, it provides the marketplace where owners discover, evaluate, book, pay, and communicate with independent pet-care providers. Rover currently advertises boarding, house sitting, drop-in visits, doggy day care, dog walking, and in-person dog training.
For example, an owner can enter their location and dates, browse sitter profiles, see reviews and rates, message candidates, arrange a Meet & Greet, and then book and pay through Rover. Sitters determine their own rates, subject to Rover's marketplace structure.
The sitter isn't generally a Rover employee. Rover  explicitly describes U.S. sitters and walkers as  independent contractors running their own small businesses .
How Rover makes money
The basic model is marketplace fees.
In the U.S., Rover's standard help documentation  says pet owners currently pay an  11% booking fee , while pet-care providers generally pay Rover a  20% service fee , taking home 80% of the booking price. Rover notes that some  providers may be in different fee pilots and that California has a different pricing structure.
There's also currently a  $49–$79 profile-review fee  for someone signing up to provide services, depending on location.
So economically, Rover has an attractive marketplace structure: it doesn't need to own kennels or employ an enormous workforce of walkers. Its main assets are the marketplace, brand, supply of sitters, customer demand, software, payments, trust/safety systems, and network effects.
The trust component is especially important
Trust is arguably the core product alongside matchmaking. Rover says providers joining its community undergo background checks, profiles contain verified reviews, bookings include 24/7 support, payments happen on-platform, and eligible bookings receive the  Rover Guarantee . Rover's U.S. site currently says the Guarantee can reimburse up to  $25,000 for eligible veterinary care .
Rover also strongly encourages owners to conduct an in-person  Meet & Greet  before booking. That's significant because a marketplace can't completely eliminate the variability between individual sitters.
Why the business is interesting
Rover has a fairly classic marketplace flywheel:
More sitters → better geographic coverage/availability → more pet owners → more bookings → greater earning opportunity → more sitters.
There are also meaningful repeat-use dynamics. Once an owner finds a sitter they trust with their dog or cat, there's a strong incentive to book  that same person again. And Rover gives owners a reason to keep those transactions on-platform through payments, messaging, support, reviews, and the Rover Guarantee.
The potential weakness is  disintermediation : after a sitter and owner meet through Rover, they could theoretically transact directly and avoid marketplace fees. Rover therefore has to make the benefits of staying on-platform—insurance/reimbursement protection, convenience, payments, support, reputation, and continued customer acquisition—valuable enough to justify the fees.
Another structural challenge is quality control. Rover is a marketplace rather than a standardized pet-care operator, so the actual experience can vary  considerably from sitter to sitter. Reviews, repeat-client statistics, background checks, Meet & Greets, and the Star Sitter program are mechanisms designed to reduce that uncertainty.
One striking scale datapoint: when Blackstone announced the acquisition in late 2023, Rover said that since inception it had facilitated  more than 93 million services , served  more than 4 million pet parents , and paid  more than 1 million pet-care providers  across North America and Europe.
If you're looking at Rover from a  business/investment/competitive-strategy perspective , I can also break down its business model, unit economics, network effects, competitive moat, main competitors, and why Blackstone was willing to pay ~$2.3B for it.

prompt: What do you know about Rover (@roverdotcom on Instagram)?
answer:
If you mean  Rover (@roverdotcom) , the pet-care company, yes—I know it. It’s a fairly substantial U.S.-founded pet-care marketplace, not just an Instagram pet-content account.
What Rover is
was founded in Seattle in 2011 by Greg Gottesman, Philip Kimmey, and Aaron Easterly. Its core business is a marketplace connecting pet owners with people who provide services such as:
• Dog walking
• Drop-in visits
• In-home pet sitting
• Dog boarding
• Doggy daycare
• Cat care
• More recently, dog training and other pet services
Rover says its mission is essentially to make it easier for people to experience the love of pets, while giving pet-care providers a way to build businesses around caring for animals.
The company today
There have been some significant changes recently.
• Aaron Easterly , the co-founder who led Rover as CEO for its first 14 years,  became Executive Chair in July 2025.
• Brent Turner , previously Rover's President and COO, became CEO.
• Rover was publicly traded under  ROVR  beginning in 2021,  but was taken private by  Blackstone  in 2024.
• In January 2026, Rover acquired  Meowtel , a cat-sitting marketplace, strengthening its push into cat care.
• Rover says it now operates across North America and Europe and has connected  6.2 million pet-owning households  with pet care.
So strategically, Rover seems to be moving beyond being simply "the dog-walking app" toward a broader  pet-care ecosystem .
And @roverdotcom specifically
Their social presence is a big part  of the brand. Rover has historically leaned heavily into  cute, emotionally resonant pet content , user-generated photos/videos, pet-owner culture,  and humorous observations about dogs and cats. That fits the business unusually well: the product itself revolves around people's emotional relationship with their pets.
If you're  asking because you're  researching Rover's Instagram account specifically —for example, its content strategy, audience, brand voice, growth, competitors, or what makes  @roverdotcom successful—I can dig into that much more deeply and break down  what they're actually doing on Instagram and why it works .

prompt: What do you know about Rover (https://www.rover.com/, @roverdotcom on Instagram)?
answer:
is a major pet-care marketplace and technology company—essentially a platform that connects pet parents with independent pet-care providers.
What Rover is
Rover was founded in  2011  and is headquartered in Seattle. Its core marketplace covers:
• Dog boarding  — overnight care at the sitter's home
• House sitting  — overnight care in the pet owner's home
• Dog walking
• Drop-in visits
• Doggy daycare
• Dog training
• More recently,  grooming/bathing  offerings in some markets
Rover describes itself as the world's largest online marketplace for pet care. Its current corporate footprint is  18 countries , with  12+ million pets cared for  and more than  41 million five-star stays  according to its own current figures.
How the business works
The interesting part is that Rover generally  doesn't employ the sitters and walkers . Instead, it operates a two-sided marketplace:
Pet parent → Rover → independent sitter/walker
A provider creates a profile, sets services/rates/availability, gets screened, and receives bookings through the platform. Pet parents can compare profiles, reviews, pricing and availability, arrange a Meet & Greet, and then book/pay through Rover.
Rover makes money by taking fees associated with transactions on its marketplace.
So strategically, it's much closer to  Airbnb/Uber for pet care  than to a traditional pet-sitting company.
Trust & safety is a big part of the product
Because Rover is facilitating access to someone's home and someone's animal, trust is central to the proposition.
Rover says it provides:
• Background checks for sitters/walkers
• Verified reviews
• In-platform messaging and payments
• 24/7 support
• A Rover Guarantee for eligible veterinary costs
• Meet & Greets before bookings
The exact protections and features vary by country and service.
That's an important distinction:  Rover is selling trust and convenience as much as it is selling pet care.
It's considerably bigger than "the dog-walking app"
Rover has been expanding aggressively beyond its original U.S. dog-sitting marketplace.
Some notable moves:
• 2024:  Blackstone completed its acquisition of Rover for approximately  $2.3 billion , taking Rover private and ending its Nasdaq listing.
• 2024:  Acquired European cat-sitting marketplace  Cat in a Flat .
• 2025:  Acquired European dog-care marketplace  Gudog  and expanded into additional European countries.
• 2025:  Completed its acquisition of Australian pet-care marketplace  Mad Paws , giving Rover a substantial Australian presence.
• 2026:  Acquired U.S. cat-sitting marketplace  Meowtel .
• 2026:  Rolled out  private dog training with credentialed trainers  in the U.S.
The broader strategy is pretty clear:  build a global, multi-service pet-care platform rather than remain a dog-sitting marketplace.
Leadership changed recently
Rover's longtime co-founder and CEO  Aaron Easterly  stepped into the role of Executive Chair in July 2025.  Brent Turner , previously President and COO and a longtime Rover executive, became CEO.
That's also notable because the company entered a new phase after going private under Blackstone.
And @roverdotcom?
The Instagram account  @roverdotcom  is Rover's consumer-facing social presence. The brand's marketing is heavily centered around the emotional relationship between people and pets—not simply the functional message of "book a dog walker."
That positioning is particularly evident in Rover's current  "We Get Your Pet"  campaign, launched in 2026, which emphasizes understanding a pet's individual personality and needs.
In other words, Rover's brand proposition is roughly:
We don't just provide pet care; we understand your pet.
That's a fairly powerful positioning for a marketplace where differentiation can otherwise devolve into price, availability, and star ratings.
One interesting thing about Rover
If you're looking at Rover from a  business, marketing, social-media, partnership, or competitive-analysis  perspective, there's quite a lot more to unpack. The company sits at an interesting intersection of  marketplace economics + creator/influencer marketing + pet culture + UGC + emotional branding + local services .
If that's why you're asking about Rover, I can also break down  their Instagram/content strategy, target audience, brand voice, business model, competitors, and what appears to be working/not working for them in 2026 .

prompt: What do you know about https://www.rover.com/ in United States?
answer:
Yes.  Rover.com  is a major U.S. online marketplace for pet care. It was founded in 2011 and is headquartered in Seattle. The basic idea is similar to a marketplace like Airbnb, but for pet care: pet owners find local independent sitters, walkers, and trainers, compare profiles/reviews/prices, and book and pay through Rover.
What Rover offers in the U.S.
• Dog boarding  — your dog stays overnight at the sitter's home.
• House sitting  — the sitter stays at your home with your pet.
• Doggy day care  — daytime care at a sitter's home.
• Dog walking  — generally 30- or 60-minute walks.
• Drop-in visits  — a sitter visits your home to feed, play with, and care for your pet.
• Dog training  — Rover launched private, in-person training with credentialed trainers across the U.S. in March 2026.
Rover is primarily designed around  dogs and cats , although individual sitters may have experience with other animals.
How the business model works
Rover isn't generally employing the sitter as a traditional pet-care employee. Instead, it operates a  two-sided marketplace :
Pet owner → Rover platform → independent pet-care provider
The provider creates a profile, chooses services, sets prices and availability, communicates with customers, and accepts bookings. Rover provides the marketplace, payment system, reviews, messaging, support, and various safety/protection features.
For customers, this means you can search by location and compare providers based on things such as reviews, experience, price, availability, and services offered. Rover recommends doing a Meet & Greet before booking with someone new.
Is Rover legitimate?
Yes.  Rover is an established pet-care marketplace rather than a random classifieds site. Rover says it operates in 18 countries and has facilitated more than 41 million five-star stays; its current U.S. site says more than 80 million pet-care services have been booked through its community.
That said,  Rover isn't a guarantee that every individual sitter is excellent . The actual care is provided by the individual provider, so choosing the right sitter is still important.
Rover says U.S. sitters and dog walkers undergo third-party criminal background checks, and profiles can show whether the person has completed a basic or enhanced check.
Safety/protection
Rover currently advertises:
• Third-party background checks for sitters and dog walkers
• Verified customer reviews
• In-platform messaging and payments
• 24/7 support
• Meet & Greet functionality
• The  Rover Guarantee , which can provide up to  $25,000 in reimbursement for eligible veterinary care  associated with a booking.
It's worth reading the actual terms of the Guarantee rather than interpreting it as conventional pet insurance—eligibility and exclusions matter.
An interesting recent development
